title: Least privilege for tools
point: Give each principal the smallest set of tools and the narrowest, shortest-lived credentials it needs, and put a human in front of anything irreversible.
definition: Least privilege for tools combines per-principal allowlists, scoped short-lived credentials, separate read and write tools, human confirmation for irreversible side effects, and no ambient credentials anywhere the agent runs.

objective.text: Given a tool catalogue and three principals, write their allowlists and credential scopes, split read from write tools, and mark which calls need human confirmation.

misconceptions.claim: One broad service account is fine if the system prompt tells the agent to be careful.
misconceptions.correction: A prompt is not a control. One injected instruction can use every permission the account holds, so scope credentials per principal and per call.

misconceptions.claim: One update_ticket tool with a mode argument is as safe as separate read and write tools.
misconceptions.correction: A combined tool forces you to grant write to anyone who needs read. Separate tools let the allowlist grant read widely and write narrowly.

l1: Per-principal allowlists: each agent or role can call only the tools it is listed for. Every other call returns DENIED.
Scoped short-lived credentials: the gateway mints a token for one tool, one principal and a few minutes. No ambient credentials sit in environment variables for model-written code to find.
Separate read tools from write tools. Require human confirmation for irreversible side effects, such as refunds, outbound emails or account deletions.
l2: A support platform has three principals: a triage bot, a support assistant and a billing assistant. The triage bot may only read tickets and orders.
The support assistant may also draft emails and change ticket status. Only the billing assistant may call refund_order, and refunds above $100 wait for a human to approve them.
Suppose a ticket injects an instruction telling the triage bot to issue a refund. The gateway returns DENIED, and the bot holds no refund credential for the injection to use.
l3: Human confirmation costs staff time. If 2 per cent of 10,000 daily refunds exceed $100, staff review 200 a day, about 3.3 hours at one minute each.
Raising the threshold to $500 might cut reviews to 40 a day, but it makes the largest unreviewed refund five times bigger.
Set the threshold from the cost of a wrong refund and the measured error rate, not from reviewer convenience, and revisit it when either changes.
